coreIdea: ∀=for all, ∃=exists. 'All A are B'→∀x(A(x)→B(x)). 'Some A are B'→∃x(A(x)∧B(x)). Quantifier ORDER matters when mixed.
mustRememberFormulas: ∃y∀xP(x,y) ⟹ ∀x∃yP(x,y), but NOT the reverse (∀∃ is weaker)

patternRecognitionTable.seeThis: English sentence → formula, or formula → English meaning
'is this valid', 'which is equivalent', negation of quantified formula

commonTrapsQuickList: Never use ∧ inside ∀ for 'all A are B' — use → (the reverse mirror trap: never use → inside ∃ for 'some')
Negating nested quantifiers: flip BOTH the quantifier type AND the inner connective
Same-type adjacent quantifiers (∀∀ or ∃∃) CAN be freely swapped
highYieldPyqLessons: Translation (15/35) and quantifier-equivalence (14/35) together are ~83% of this topic — master just these two skills for near-full coverage.
The ∀∃ vs ∃∀ non-equivalence has been tested in some form almost every 2-3 GATE cycles — a guaranteed-recurring trap worth memorizing cold.
